intro: Protection only works if someone pays for it, the money arrives in time, and it is still there next season. Start from what needs paying for, not from a product.

needs.need: Shade, cooler buildings and water points
needs.route: Public investment, grants or infrastructure finance
needs.ask: Who pays to build it, and who pays to run it afterwards?

needs.route: Recurring public, employer or programme budgets
needs.ask: Is the money there every season, not just the first?
Can money be released before people are harmed?

needs.route: Cash assistance, contingency reserves or suitable insurance
needs.ask: Will money arrive before people borrow or go back to unsafe work?

needs.route: Social protection and affordable essential services
needs.ask: What keeps supporting them between heatwaves?

needsNote: A way to compare routes, not a claim that every route exists in every country.

triggers.name: Warning trigger
triggers.does: Prompts an official heat advisory or warning.
triggers.who: Usually the weather service, often with health authorities

triggers.name: Action trigger
triggers.does: Switches on agreed measures: outreach, rest breaks, cooling spaces open.
triggers.who: The heat plan’s lead office and each department

triggers.name: Payout trigger
triggers.does: Decides whether a specific insurance contract pays.
triggers.who: Set in the contract; the insurer or a calculation agent confirms it

triggersNote: The three need not match. Protective action works best when it does not wait for an insurance payout.

basis.q: Why can someone lose income to heat and get no payout?

kinds.name: Wrong place
kinds.text: The contract measures heat at a weather station or grid point, but the workplace or home is hotter.

kinds.name: Wrong measure
kinds.text: The index counts temperature, but humidity, heavy work or hot nights caused the harm.

kinds.name: Wrong amount
kinds.text: It pays, but a fixed amount that covers only part of what was lost.

basis.ask: If the contract does not pay, what support is still there?
basis.note: Clear explanation prevents disappointment when a contract works as designed. It cannot fix a contract that leaves real losses uncovered.

source.label: Global Asia Insurance Partnership, Scaling Parametric Insurance in Asia, 2026, pp. 48–51

steps: People receive support they can use
pathway.note: When money goes first to a government, cooperative or microfinance institution, someone still has to decide who gets it. Count the date at every step, not only the day the insurer pays.

source.label: Global Asia Insurance Partnership, Scaling Parametric Insurance in Asia, 2026, pp. 52–53

fields.name: Who receives the money first
fields.placeholder: e.g. the city disaster fund, a workers’ cooperative

fields.name: Who it is meant to reach
fields.placeholder: e.g. registered street vendors in three wards

fields.name: How it is shared out
fields.placeholder: e.g. a fixed amount per registered member

fields.name: When it is needed
fields.placeholder: e.g. within 3 days of a red alert

fields.name: How it is paid, and the fallback
fields.placeholder: e.g. mobile wallet; cash at the ward office

fields.name: Where people can complain
fields.placeholder: e.g. a helpline run by the workers’ union

fields.name: What is still not covered
fields.placeholder: e.g. workers outside the scheme; losses above the payout

survive: Who pays next year’s premium and running costs?
What happens when donor money ends?
Who keeps the knowledge when staff change?
How will you review seasons with a payout, and without one?
What evidence would make you change it, or stop it?

surviveSource.label: Global Asia Insurance Partnership, Scaling Parametric Insurance in Asia, 2026, pp. 58–59

boundary: These reports describe how insurance is regulated, designed and delivered in Asia. The parametric report did not assess consumer outcomes, pricing, contracts or how triggers performed, so it supports design questions, not proof that a heat product works.

boundarySource.label: Global Asia Insurance Partnership, Scaling Parametric Insurance in Asia, 2026, pp. 14–15

lenders.title: When heat reaches lenders
lenders.intro: Heat does not stop at the household. When people earn less in a heatwave, loan repayments slow, and the strain travels up to microfinance institutions and banks. A 2026 commentary sets out how, and what could help.
facts: Heatwaves in 2025 reduced how much lenders collected in the June quarter across loan books that depend on field visits, with a similar squeeze projected for 2026 in northern and central India.
About 60% of India’s ₹3.81 trillion microfinance portfolio is in agriculture and allied activities, and eastern India, among the most climate-vulnerable regions, holds roughly a third of it.

The borrowers most exposed (microfinance clients, farming households, gold-loan borrowers and self-employed informal workers) are also the most financially vulnerable, because their income depends on outdoor work and moving around.
When collections slow, lenders face a cash crunch of their own and turn to costlier short-term funding; branch closures and fewer field visits in hot zones add to the strain.

The Reserve Bank of India now treats heatwaves as a prudential risk, and draft climate-risk disclosure directions ask banks to map and stress-test heat exposure, though compliance remains voluntary for some.
At least one large public-sector bank now counts heat among 13 key climate hazards and is building sector-by-sector vulnerability tools.

helps.name: Parametric insurance
helps.text: Payouts that arrive automatically when heat crosses a set threshold, so informal workers and smallholders have a buffer against lost income. SEWA’s heat cover for women informal workers is the leading Indian example.

helps.name: Blended finance
helps.text: Concessional or patient capital that takes early risk so commercial money can follow, for example into near-farm storage that cuts heat spoilage and lets farmers avoid distress sales.

helps.name: Green and resilience bonds
helps.text: Large, long-term capital for resilient public buildings, water and urban infrastructure; Indonesia’s sovereign Green Sukuk has raised over US$10 billion since 2018 for climate-resilient projects.

helps.name: Shared heat-risk data
helps.text: Standard, location-specific heat-risk information, such as the RBI’s Climate Risk Information System, so lenders can assess exposure without each building their own.

helps.name: Lending tied to heat outcomes
helps.text: Loan terms linked to measurable results such as lower indoor temperatures, lower peak power demand or more cool-roof coverage, rather than broad ESG scores.

helps.name: City-level financing platforms
helps.text: Pooling many small projects, such as cool roofs and efficient cooling for public buildings, into portfolios that banks and investors can finance, as municipal rooftop-solar bonds have done in Surat and New Delhi.

lenders.shift: The commentary’s central point: the financial system needs to move from financing vulnerability to financing resilience.

source.label: Namita Vikas, commentary, Mongabay India, 29 June 2026

lenders.note: A commentary: the views are the author’s. Figures are as reported there, with links to the original sources in the article.

cases.name: Heat income cover for women informal workers
cases.paid: Premiums were paid largely by Climate Resilience for All, with members contributing; reported amounts differ by source and year.
cases.received: Members of the Self Employed Women’s Association (SEWA). Swiss Re reported more than 46,000 women paid after the May 2024 heatwaves.
cases.enabled: Cash for lost working days, alongside early warnings and low-cost protection such as shade tarps and cooling boxes.
cases.uncovered: The 2023 pilot’s threshold was set too high, so women got nothing on very hot days until it was lowered. In 2025 most payments were reported to take six to eight weeks.
cases.continued: Grew from about 21,000 women in the 2023 pilot to 50,000 by 2025. No independent evaluation found.
cases.lesson: Insurance worked as one part of a package. The threshold and the payment speed decide whether money helps when it is needed.

sources.label: Global Asia Insurance Partnership, Physical risks on the insurance industry, 2026, p. 13
Swiss Re: the structure behind a parametric solution for SEWA
NPR, 16 July 2025: on super hot days, this insurance plan pays out cash for lost wages

cases.name: Government cover that switched to its own disaster data
cases.hazard: Floods and other disasters, not heat
cases.paid: The Government of Lao PDR, through the Southeast Asia Disaster Risk Insurance Facility (SEADRIF).
cases.received: The government, for emergency response and budget planning.
cases.enabled: The first policy paid on a modelled count of people affected, which kept disagreeing with the government’s own figures. The renewed 2025–2027 policy pays on the national disaster office’s reported impact data, up to US$8 million a year. A US$2 million payout was made in September 2025, six days after the figures were finalised.
cases.uncovered: The report does not describe how the money then reached affected families.
cases.lesson: Trust grows when the trigger uses data the government already relies on to run its response. A lesson about data, not heat evidence.

sources.label: Global Asia Insurance Partnership, Scaling Parametric Insurance in Asia, 2026, p. 51

cases.name: Pay for days too dangerous to work
cases.hazard: Wind, waves and rain, not heat
cases.paid: The Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources pays the premiums from its budget, as the policyholder.
cases.received: About 14,200 registered small-scale fishers, up to US$100 per policy cycle.
cases.enabled: Income when weather makes fishing unsafe: it insures lost working days, not damaged boats.
cases.uncovered: Thresholds are not public, and results have not yet been reported; it launched in November 2025.
cases.lesson: The same logic heat income cover needs: pay for days too dangerous to work, with a public agency as policyholder so people who would never buy cover are reached.

sources.label: Global Asia Insurance Partnership, Scaling Parametric Insurance in Asia, 2026, p. 50
